title: Convolution dual action detects subcomodules and comodule maps
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $C$ be a $k$-vector space with $k$-linear maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_k C$ and $\epsilon:C\to k$ satisfying coassociativity and both counit identities. Tensor products have the meaning of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Let $A=\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,k)$ with its convolution algebra structure [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra]: $(f*g)(c)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta c)$ and $1_A=\epsilon$. A right $C$-comodule is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a linear map $\rho_M:M\to M\otimes_k C$ satisfying $(\rho_M\otimes1_C)\rho_M=(1_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$ and $(1_M\otimes\epsilon)\rho_M=1_M$, under the canonical tensor identifications. For every such comodule, the operators $T_f^M=(1_M\otimes f)\rho_M$, identifying $M\otimes_k k$ with $M$, define a unital $k$-algebra homomorphism $A\to\operatorname{End}_k(M)$; in particular $T_{f*g}^M=T_f^M\circ T_g^M$ and $T_{a\epsilon}^M=a\,1_M$. For every $k$-linear subspace $W\subseteq M$ with inclusion $i$, $T_f^M(W)\subseteq W$ for all $f\in A$ if and only if there is a linear map $\rho_W:W\to W\otimes_k C$ with $(i\otimes1_C)\rho_W=\rho_Mi$; this map is unique and satisfies both comodule identities. For any two right $C$-comodules $M,N$, a $k$-linear map $u:M\to N$ satisfies $(u\otimes1_C)\rho_M=\rho_Nu$ if and only if $uT_f^M=T_f^Nu$ for every $f\in A$. No finite-dimensionality or cocommutativity of $C,M,N$ is assumed; zero coalgebras and zero comodules are allowed.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual algebra and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178, gives the finite-dimensional duality special case. General contraction-detection formulation supplied by Q09.

proof.text: Write $\rho_M(m)=\sum_i m_i\otimes c_i$, with finite sums. Tensor bilinearity makes $f\mapsto T_f^M$ linear. By coassociativity, $\sum_i\rho_M(m_i)\otimes c_i=\sum_i m_i\otimes\Delta(c_i)$. Applying $1_M\otimes f\otimes g$ gives $T_f^M(T_g^M(m))=\sum_i m_i(f*g)(c_i)=T_{f*g}^M(m)$, in exactly this order. The counit identity gives $T_\epsilon^M=1_M$; linearity gives $T_{a\epsilon}^M=a1_M$. Together with the cited convolution algebra, these verify every algebra-homomorphism law.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178. General detection argument supplied by Q25.

proof.text: For later use, contractions detect zero in $X\otimes_k C$ for every vector space $X$: if $(1_X\otimes f)t=0$ for all $f:C\to k$, then $t=0$. Indeed, the dual-separation statement says these $f$ detect zero in $C$. Apply the tensor-family statement with its $M=C$, $N=X$, $J=\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,k)$, $P_f=k$ to the flip of $t$. The flip and $k\otimes X\cong X$ come directly from the tensor universal property; on $x\otimes c$ the resulting map is $f(c)x$. Thus all the hypotheses of that statement hold, without any dimension restriction.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178. General detection argument supplied by Q25.

proof.text: Choose a complement $Q$ to $W$ in $M$. The unique decomposition $m=i(w)+q$ defines a linear projection $p:M\to W$, $p(i(w)+q)=w$. Its linearity follows by adding decompositions and multiplying them by scalars, then using uniqueness. Thus $pi=1_W$. Put $r=1_M-ip$; then $ri=0$ and $\ker r=i(W)$. In particular $i\otimes1_D$ is injective for every vector space $D$, since $p\otimes1_D$ is a left inverse: the composite sends $w\otimes d$ to itself, hence is the identity by tensor generation.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178. General detection argument supplied by Q25.

proof.text: Assume all $T_f^M$ preserve $W$. For $w\in W$, every contraction of $t=(r\otimes1_C)\rho_M(iw)$ equals $rT_f^M(iw)=0$, so step 2 gives $t=0$. Define the linear map $\rho_W=(p\otimes1_C)\rho_M i$. Then $(i\otimes1_C)\rho_W=\rho_M i$, since their difference is $(r\otimes1_C)\rho_M i=0$. Conversely, any map with this factorization gives $T_f^M i=i(1_W\otimes f)\rho_W$, whose image lies in $i(W)$. These equalities follow on pure tensors from the universal property. Finally applying $p\otimes1_C$ to any such factorization forces the displayed formula for $\rho_W$, proving uniqueness.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178. General detection argument supplied by Q25.

proof.text: The factorization from step 4 implies the counit law: applying $i$ to $(1_W\otimes\epsilon)\rho_W$ gives $(1_M\otimes\epsilon)\rho_M i=i$, and cancel $i$ using $p$. For coassociativity, apply $i\otimes1_C\otimes1_C$ to the two maps $(\rho_W\otimes1_C)\rho_W$ and $(1_W\otimes\Delta)\rho_W$. The first becomes $(\rho_M\otimes1_C)\rho_M i$, using the factorization twice; the second becomes $(1_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M i$, using it once. They agree by coassociativity of $\rho_M$. Cancel $i\otimes1_{C\otimes C}$ using $p\otimes1_{C\otimes C}$ as in step 3. All associativity and composition identifications here agree on pure tensors.

source.place: Chapter 9(d), printed pp.174–175, coalgebra dual and comodule identities; Example 9.36, printed p.178. General detection argument supplied by Q25.

proof.text: For a linear map $u:M\to N$, set $d=(u\otimes1_C)\rho_M-\rho_Nu$. Its contraction by $f$ is $uT_f^M-T_f^Nu$, as follows by evaluating on pure tensors. If $d=0$ this gives every intertwining identity. Conversely, if all intertwining identities hold, apply step 2 to $d(m)\in N\otimes C$ for each $m\in M$: all its contractions vanish, so $d(m)=0$. Thus $d=0$, exactly the comodule-map identity. This argument uses the full algebraic dual and therefore also applies to infinite-dimensional $C,M,N$.
